13	### Equipartition criterion
14	
15	For \(j\) absolutely continuous probability measures on \(\mathbb R^d\), two hyperplanes simultaneously equipartition all of them whenever
16	\[
17	x^j y^j(x+y)^j\ne0
18	\quad\text{in}\quad
19	\mathbb F_2[x,y]/(x^{d+1},y^{d+1}).
20	\tag{1}
21	\]
22	
23	To prove this, parametrize oriented affine hyperplanes by
24	\[
25	a=(a_0,\ldots,a_d)\in S^d,\qquad
26	\ell_a(z)=a_0+\sum_{r=1}^d a_rz_r.
27	\]
28	The two poles represent constant positive and negative functions. Write
29	\(\epsilon_a(z)=\operatorname{sgn}\ell_a(z)\). For each measure \(\mu_i\), define
30	\[
31	f_i(a,b)=\int\epsilon_a\,d\mu_i,\quad
32	g_i(a,b)=\int\epsilon_b\,d\mu_i,\quad
33	h_i(a,b)=\int\epsilon_a\epsilon_b\,d\mu_i.
34	\]
35	These functions are continuous by dominated convergence, including at the poles.
36	
37	Under \(a\mapsto-a\), the functions \(f_i,h_i\) change sign; under \(b\mapsto-b\), the functions \(g_i,h_i\) change sign. Consequently, together they define a section of
38	\[
39	E=L_x^{\oplus j}\oplus L_y^{\oplus j}
40	       \oplus(L_x\otimes L_y)^{\oplus j}
41	\]
42	over \(\mathbb RP^d\times\mathbb RP^d\), where \(L_x,L_y\) are the two tautological line bundles.
43	
44	Here are the standard characteristic-class facts used in this argument:
45	\[
46	H^*(\mathbb RP^d\times\mathbb RP^d;\mathbb F_2)
47	=\mathbb F_2[x,y]/(x^{d+1},y^{d+1}),
48	\]
49	\[
50	w_1(L_x)=x,\quad w_1(L_y)=y,\quad
51	w_1(L_x\otimes L_y)=x+y.
52	\]
53	The Whitney product formula therefore gives
54	\[
55	w_{3j}(E)=x^jy^j(x+y)^j.
56	\]
57	A nowhere-zero section would split off a trivial line bundle, forcing this top Stiefel–Whitney class to vanish. Thus (1) forces a zero of the section.
58	
59	At such a zero, the mass of the sign region \((\alpha,\beta)\in\{\pm1\}^2\) is
60	\[
61	\frac14\left(1+\alpha f_i+\beta g_i+\alpha\beta h_i\right)=\frac14.
62	\]
63	Neither parameter is a pole. All four sign regions are nonempty and convex, so they are exactly the four connected components required in the question. This proves the criterion.
64	
65	### Applying the criterion
66

68	\[
69	n=2^{s-1},\qquad j=2n-2,\qquad d=3n-2.
70	\]

73	x^jy^j(x+y)^j
74	=\sum_k\binom jk x^{j+k}y^{2j-k},
75	\]
76	take \(k=n-2\). The resulting monomial is
77	\[
78	x^{3n-4}y^{3n-2}=x^{d-2}y^d.
79	\]
80	Its coefficient is odd. Indeed, over \(\mathbb F_2\),
81	\[
82	(1+t)^{2^s-2}=\prod_{r=1}^{s-1}(1+t^{2^r}),
83	\]
84	and \(n-2=2+4+\cdots+2^{s-2}\) occurs exactly once.
85

87	\[
88	D_s\le 3n-2.
89	\tag{2}
90	\]

92	## 2. Positive-definite bilinear forms with no common orthogonal pair
93	
94	The following explicit construction supplies the stronger lower bound.
95	
96	### Lemma
97	
98	For every even \(n\ge4\), there exist \(2n-2\) real symmetric positive-definite \(n\times n\) matrices
99	\[
100	A_0,\ldots,A_{2n-3}
101	\]
102	such that
103	\[
104	u^{\mathsf T}A_i v=0\quad\text{for every }i
105	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=0\text{ or }v=0.
106	\tag{3}
107	\]
108	
109	### Proof
110	
111	Write \(n=2m\), where \(m\ge2\), and identify \(\mathbb R^n\) with the real vector space
112	\[
113	V=\mathbb C[t]_{\le m-1}.
114	\]
115	
116	Choose the following \(2m-2\) distinct positive integers:
117	\[
118	R=\{3\}\cup\{\,4r+1:0\le r\le2m-4\,\},
119	\]
120	and put
121	\[
122	P(t)=\prod_{r\in R}(t+r).
123	\]
124	All roots are simple, and all coefficients of \(P\) are positive.
125	
126	We need one useful property of its complementary factors. If
127	\[
128	P=FG,\qquad \deg F=\deg G=m-1,
129	\]
130	with \(F,G\) monic, then
131	\[
132	F(0)G(1)-F(1)G(0)\ne0.
133	\tag{4}
134	\]
135	To see this, let \(v_2\) denote the exponent of \(2\) in a nonzero rational number. Each \(4r+1\) contributes \(1\) to
136	\(v_2(P(1)/P(0))\), while the exceptional integer \(3\) contributes \(2\). Hence
137	\[
138	v_2\!\left(\frac{P(1)}{P(0)}\right)
139	=(2m-3)+2=2m-1,
140	\tag{5}
141	\]
142	which is odd. Equality in the negation of (4) would give
143	\[
144	\frac{F(1)}{F(0)}=\frac{G(1)}{G(0)},
145	\]
146	making (5) twice an integer, a contradiction.
147	
148	We now define \(4m-2=2n-2\) real symmetric bilinear forms on \(V\):
149	
150	* the coefficient inner product
151	  \[
152	  b_0(U,V)=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\overline{u_k}v_k;
153	  \]
154	* the form
155	  \[
156	  b_1(U,V)=
157	  \operatorname{Re}\!\left(
158	    i\bigl(\overline{U(0)}V(1)-\overline{U(1)}V(0)\bigr)
159	  \right);
160	  \]
161	* the real and imaginary parts of each of the \(2m-2\) coefficients of the remainder of \(UV\) modulo \(P\).
162	
163	The last forms are symmetric because polynomial multiplication is commutative. The form \(b_1\) is also real symmetric: its complex matrix is \(iK\), where \(K\) is real skew-symmetric.
164	
165	We claim these forms have no common zero on a pair of nonzero vectors. Suppose otherwise. The remainder conditions give
166	\[
167	UV=cP.
168	\]
169	Since \(U,V\ne0\), we have \(c\ne0\). Degree considerations and unique factorization give
170	\[
171	U=aF,\qquad V=bG,
172	\]
173	where \(a,b\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\), and \(F,G\) are complementary monic degree-\((m-1)\) factors of \(P\).
174	
175	Their coefficients are positive, so
176	\[
177	C=\sum_k F_kG_k>0.
178	\]
179	Thus \(b_0(U,V)=0\) gives
180	\[
181	\operatorname{Re}(\overline ab)=0.
182	\]
183	By (4), the equation \(b_1(U,V)=0\) gives
184	\[
185	\operatorname{Im}(\overline ab)=0.
186	\]
187	This contradicts \(a,b\ne0\).
188	
189	Finally, \(b_0\) is positive definite. Replace every other form \(b\) by
190	\[
191	b+M b_0
192	\]
193	with \(M\) sufficiently large that the replacement is positive definite. Keep \(b_0\) itself. Common vanishing is unchanged, since the equation \(b_0(U,V)=0\) is retained. The resulting matrices satisfy (3). ∎
194	
195	## 3. Gaussian counterexamples
196	
197	Take
198	\[
199	n=2^{s-1},\qquad j=2n-2,\qquad d_0=j+n-1=3n-3.
200	\]
201	Use the matrices from the lemma, indexed \(A_0,\ldots,A_{j-1}\).
202	
203	Decompose
204	\[
205	\mathbb R^{d_0}=\mathbb R^{j-1}\oplus\mathbb R^n.
206	\]
207	Choose Gaussian probability measures \(\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_{j-1}\) with means
208	\[
209	c_0=0,\qquad c_r=(e_r,0)\quad(1\le r\le j-1)
210	\]
211	and covariance matrices
212	\[
213	\Sigma_i=
214	\begin{pmatrix}
215	I_{j-1}&0\\
216	0&A_i
217	\end{pmatrix}.
218	\tag{6}
219	\]
220	These are nondegenerate Gaussians, hence absolutely continuous.
221	
222	Suppose two affine hyperplanes equipartition all these measures. Each hyperplane must bisect every measure.
223	
224	A hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it passes through its mean: its defining affine functional is a one-dimensional normal random variable, whose unique median is its mean. Consequently, each of our hyperplanes contains all the \(c_i\). Its equation therefore has the form
225	\[
226	u^{\mathsf T}z=0,\qquad u\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}.
227	\]
228	Write the two normals as \(u,v\).
229	
230	For centered jointly normal random variables \(Y,Z\) of correlation \(\rho\),
231	\[
232	\Pr(Y>0,Z>0)=\frac14+\frac{\arcsin\rho}{2\pi}.
233	\tag{7}
234	\]
235	For example, (7) follows by expressing \(Y,Z\) as two linear functionals of an isotropic planar Gaussian and measuring the angle of the intersection of their positive halfplanes. Thus all four sign probabilities equal \(1/4\) only if \(\rho=0\).
236	
237	Applied to (6), this implies
238	\[
239	u^{\mathsf T}A_i v=0\qquad(0\le i\le j-1).
240	\]
241	The lemma says that \(u=0\) or \(v=0\), a contradiction.
242	
243	Hence the desired property fails in dimension \(d_0=3n-3\).
244	
245	The property is monotone in dimension: project measures in a larger-dimensional space onto a smaller-dimensional space, apply the property there, and lift the hyperplanes. The projected measures remain absolutely continuous by Fubini’s theorem. Therefore failure in dimension \(d_0\) implies
246	\[
247	D_s\ge d_0+1=3n-2.
248	\tag{8}
249	\]
250	Together, (2) and (8) prove the formula.
251	
252	## 4. Exact Python checks
253	
254	The following code constructs the matrices exactly, checks positive definiteness by strict diagonal dominance, checks the polynomial-remainder identities, and exhaustively checks all complementary factorizations for \(s=3,4,5\). It also constructs the Gaussian means and covariances.
255	
256	These finite computations verify the explicit construction; the arguments above establish it for every \(s\).
257	
258	```python
259	import itertools
260	from math import comb
261	import sympy as S
262	
263	
264	def v2(a):
265	    a = int(a)
266	    result = 0
267	    while a % 2 == 0:
268	        a //= 2
269	        result += 1
270	    return result
271	
272	
273	def matrices(s):
274	    assert s >= 3
275	    n = 2**(s - 1)
276	    m = n // 2
277	    j = 2*n - 2
278	    t = S.Symbol("t")
279	
280	    roots = [3] + [4*i + 1 for i in range(2*m - 3)]
281	    P = S.Poly(S.prod(t + r for r in roots), t)
282	
283	    assert len(set(roots)) == 2*m - 2
284	    assert P.degree() == 2*m - 2
285	    assert v2(P.eval(1)) - v2(P.eval(0)) == 2*m - 1
286	
287	    Z = S.zeros(m)
288	    B, Ts = [], []
289	
290	    # T_ell gives coefficient ell of UV modulo P.
291	    for ell in range(2*m - 2):
292	        T = S.Matrix(m, m, lambda a, b: int(a + b == ell))
293	        T[m-1, m-1] -= P.nth(ell)
294	        Ts.append(T)
295	
296	        # Real and imaginary parts of the complex bilinear form.
297	        B.append(S.diag(T, -T))
298	        B.append(Z.row_join(T).col_join(T.row_join(Z)))
299	
300	    e0 = S.zeros(m, 1)
301	    e0[0] = 1
302	    e1 = S.ones(m, 1)
303	    K = e0*e1.T - e1*e0.T
304	    B.append(Z.row_join(-K).col_join(K.row_join(Z)))
305	
306	    I = S.eye(n)
307	    A = [I]
308	    for b in B:
309	        assert b == b.T
310	        shift = 1 + max(
311	            sum(abs(b[r, c]) for c in range(n))
312	            for r in range(n)
313	        )
314	        a = b + shift*I
315	
316	        # Symmetric strict diagonal dominance with positive diagonal
317	        # proves positive definiteness.
318	        assert all(
319	            a[r, r] > sum(
320	                abs(a[r, c]) for c in range(n) if c != r
321	            )
322	            for r in range(n)
323	        )
324	        A.append(a)
325	
326	    assert len(A) == j
327	
328	    # Check all polynomial-remainder identities on a bilinear basis.
329	    for a in range(m):
330	        for b in range(m):
331	            remainder = S.rem(t**(a+b), P.as_expr(), t)
332	            reconstructed = sum(
333	                Ts[ell][a, b]*t**ell
334	                for ell in range(2*m - 2)
335	            )
336	            assert S.expand(remainder - reconstructed) == 0
337	
338	    return roots, P, K, A
339	
340	
341	def check_factors(roots, P, K):
342	    m = K.rows
343	    t = P.gen
344	    count = 0
345	
346	    for indices in itertools.combinations(range(len(roots)), m-1):
347	        # One representative of each complementary pair.
348	        if 0 not in indices:
349	            continue
350	        indices = set(indices)
351	
352	        f = S.Poly(S.prod(t + roots[i] for i in indices), t)
353	        g = S.Poly(S.prod(
354	            t + roots[i]
355	            for i in range(len(roots)) if i not in indices
356	        ), t)
357	
358	        u = S.Matrix([f.nth(i) for i in range(m)])
359	        v = S.Matrix([g.nth(i) for i in range(m)])
360	
361	        assert f*g == P
362	        assert (u.T*v)[0] > 0
363	
364	        w = (u.T*K*v)[0]
365	        assert w == f.eval(0)*g.eval(1) - f.eval(1)*g.eval(0)
366	        assert w != 0
367	        count += 1
368	
369	    assert count == comb(2*m - 2, m-1)//2
370	    return count
371	
372	
373	def check_upper(s):
374	    n = 2**(s-1)
375	    j, d, k = 2*n - 2, 3*n - 2, n - 2
376	    assert j + k == d - 2
377	    assert 2*j - k == d
378	
379	    # Binary criterion for an odd binomial coefficient.
380	    assert (k & ~j) == 0
381	    if s <= 12:
382	        assert comb(j, k) % 2 == 1
383	    return d
384	
385	
386	for s in range(3, 21):
387	    check_upper(s)
388	print("Upper-bound coefficient checked for s=3,...,20.")
389	
390	for s in (3, 4, 5):
391	    roots, P, K, A = matrices(s)
392	    pairs = check_factors(roots, P, K)
393	    n, j = A[0].rows, len(A)
394	    print(
395	        f"s={s}: n={n}, {j} SPD matrices; "
396	        f"{pairs} complementary factor pairs checked; "
397	        f"D={check_upper(s)}"
398	    )
399	
400	    # Construct and check the Gaussian data.
401	    d0 = j + n - 1
402	    means = [S.zeros(d0, 1)]
403	    for k in range(j-1):
404	        c = S.zeros(d0, 1)
405	        c[k] = 1
406	        means.append(c)
407	
408	    assert S.Matrix.hstack(*means[1:]).rank() == j-1
409	
410	    for a in A:
411	        covariance = S.diag(S.eye(j-1), a)
412	        assert covariance.shape == (d0, d0)
413	        assert covariance[j-1:, j-1:] == a
414	        assert all(
415	            covariance[r, r] > sum(
416	                abs(covariance[r, c])
417	                for c in range(d0) if c != r
418	            )
419	            for r in range(d0)
420	        )
421	
422	print(
423	    "Gaussian counterexample data checked exactly "
424	    "in dimensions 9, 21, 45."
425	)

91	
92	The following explicit construction supplies the stronger lower bound.
93	
94	### Lemma
95	
96	For every even \(n\ge4\), there exist \(2n-2\) real symmetric positive-definite \(n\times n\) matrices
97	\[
98	A_0,\ldots,A_{2n-3}
99	\]
100	such that
101	\[
102	u^{\mathsf T}A_i v=0\quad\text{for every }i
103	\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u=0\text{ or }v=0.
104	\tag{3}
105	\]
106	
107	### Proof
108	
109	Write \(n=2m\), where \(m\ge2\), and identify \(\mathbb R^n\) with the real vector space
110	\[
111	V=\mathbb C[t]_{\le m-1}.
112	\]
113	
114	Choose the following \(2m-2\) distinct positive integers:
115	\[
116	R=\{3\}\cup\{\,4r+1:0\le r\le2m-4\,\},
117	\]
118	and put
119	\[
120	P(t)=\prod_{r\in R}(t+r).
121	\]
122	All roots are simple, and all coefficients of \(P\) are positive.
123	
124	We need one useful property of its complementary factors. If
125	\[
126	P=FG,\qquad \deg F=\deg G=m-1,
127	\]
128	with \(F,G\) monic, then
129	\[
130	F(0)G(1)-F(1)G(0)\ne0.
131	\tag{4}
132	\]
133	To see this, let \(v_2\) denote the exponent of \(2\) in a nonzero rational number. Each \(4r+1\) contributes \(1\) to
134	\(v_2(P(1)/P(0))\), while the exceptional integer \(3\) contributes \(2\). Hence
135	\[
136	v_2\!\left(\frac{P(1)}{P(0)}\right)
137	=(2m-3)+2=2m-1,
138	\tag{5}
139	\]
140	which is odd. Equality in the negation of (4) would give
141	\[
142	\frac{F(1)}{F(0)}=\frac{G(1)}{G(0)},
143	\]
144	making (5) twice an integer, a contradiction.
145	
146	We now define \(4m-2=2n-2\) real symmetric bilinear forms on \(V\):
147	
148	* the coefficient inner product
149	  \[
150	  b_0(U,V)=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\overline{u_k}v_k;
151	  \]
152	* the form
153	  \[
154	  b_1(U,V)=
155	  \operatorname{Re}\!\left(
156	    i\bigl(\overline{U(0)}V(1)-\overline{U(1)}V(0)\bigr)
157	  \right);
158	  \]
159	* the real and imaginary parts of each of the \(2m-2\) coefficients of the remainder of \(UV\) modulo \(P\).
160	
161	The last forms are symmetric because polynomial multiplication is commutative. The form \(b_1\) is also real symmetric: its complex matrix is \(iK\), where \(K\) is real skew-symmetric.
162	
163	We claim these forms have no common zero on a pair of nonzero vectors. Suppose otherwise. The remainder conditions give
164	\[
165	UV=cP.
166	\]
167	Since \(U,V\ne0\), we have \(c\ne0\). Degree considerations and unique factorization give
168	\[
169	U=aF,\qquad V=bG,
170	\]
171	where \(a,b\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\), and \(F,G\) are complementary monic degree-\((m-1)\) factors of \(P\).
172	
173	Their coefficients are positive, so
174	\[
175	C=\sum_k F_kG_k>0.
176	\]
177	Thus \(b_0(U,V)=0\) gives
178	\[
179	\operatorname{Re}(\overline ab)=0.
180	\]
181	By (4), the equation \(b_1(U,V)=0\) gives
182	\[
183	\operatorname{Im}(\overline ab)=0.
184	\]
185	This contradicts \(a,b\ne0\).
186	
187	Finally, \(b_0\) is positive definite. Replace every other form \(b\) by
188	\[
189	b+M b_0
190	\]
191	with \(M\) sufficiently large that the replacement is positive definite. Keep \(b_0\) itself. Common vanishing is unchanged, since the equation \(b_0(U,V)=0\) is retained. The resulting matrices satisfy (3). ∎

193	## 3. Gaussian counterexamples
194	
195	Take
196	\[
197	n=2^{s-1},\qquad j=2n-2,\qquad d_0=j+n-1=3n-3.
198	\]
199	Use the matrices from the lemma, indexed \(A_0,\ldots,A_{j-1}\).
200	
201	Decompose
202	\[
203	\mathbb R^{d_0}=\mathbb R^{j-1}\oplus\mathbb R^n.
204	\]
205	Choose Gaussian probability measures \(\mu_0,\ldots,\mu_{j-1}\) with means
206	\[
207	c_0=0,\qquad c_r=(e_r,0)\quad(1\le r\le j-1)
208	\]
209	and covariance matrices
210	\[
211	\Sigma_i=
212	\begin{pmatrix}
213	I_{j-1}&0\\
214	0&A_i
215	\end{pmatrix}.
216	\tag{6}
217	\]
218	These are nondegenerate Gaussians, hence absolutely continuous.
219	
220	Suppose two affine hyperplanes equipartition all these measures. Each hyperplane must bisect every measure.
221	
222	A hyperplane bisects a nondegenerate Gaussian exactly when it passes through its mean: its defining affine functional is a one-dimensional normal random variable, whose unique median is its mean. Consequently, each of our hyperplanes contains all the \(c_i\). Its equation therefore has the form
223	\[
224	u^{\mathsf T}z=0,\qquad u\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}.
225	\]
226	Write the two normals as \(u,v\).
227	
228	For centered jointly normal random variables \(Y,Z\) of correlation \(\rho\),
229	\[
230	\Pr(Y>0,Z>0)=\frac14+\frac{\arcsin\rho}{2\pi}.
231	\tag{7}
232	\]
233	For example, (7) follows by expressing \(Y,Z\) as two linear functionals of an isotropic planar Gaussian and measuring the angle of the intersection of their positive halfplanes. Thus all four sign probabilities equal \(1/4\) only if \(\rho=0\).
234	
235	Applied to (6), this implies
236	\[
237	u^{\mathsf T}A_i v=0\qquad(0\le i\le j-1).
238	\]
239	The lemma says that \(u=0\) or \(v=0\), a contradiction.
240	
241	Hence the desired property fails in dimension \(d_0=3n-3\).
242	
243	The property is monotone in dimension: project measures in a larger-dimensional space onto a smaller-dimensional space, apply the property there, and lift the hyperplanes. The projected measures remain absolutely continuous by Fubini’s theorem. Therefore failure in dimension \(d_0\) implies
244	\[
245	D_s\ge d_0+1=3n-2.
246	\tag{8}
247	\]
248	Together, (2) and (8) prove the formula.
